nameStory: The Cross-hatched Lucine gets its name from the distinctive pattern of intersecting lines that crisscross its shell surface, creating a grid-like design that looks like an artist's cross-hatching technique. The "lucine" part comes from the Latin word "lucina," meaning "bringing to light," possibly referring to how these pale shells stand out against dark sand when washed ashore.
description: The Cross-hatched Lucine is a small, round clam with a distinctive sculptured shell that looks like it's been etched with a fine grid pattern. These marine bivalves typically grow to about 1-2 inches across and have thick, sturdy white to cream-colored shells. Like other clams, they live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms, filtering tiny food particles from the water through their siphons. You're most likely to encounter their empty shells washed up on New England beaches after storms.

idTips.label: Cross-hatched pattern
idTips.description: The shell surface features distinct intersecting ridges that create a grid or cross-hatched pattern you can feel with your fingertip - this texture is rougher than most smooth clam shells

idTips.label: Round shell shape
idTips.description: Nearly circular outline when viewed from above, much rounder than the oval shape of most common clams like quahogs

idTips.label: Shell thickness
idTips.description: Noticeably thick and heavy for its size - feels solid and substantial in your palm, not delicate like razor clam shells

idTips.label: Color and surface
idTips.description: Typically white to pale cream colored, sometimes with a chalky texture that may leave a slight residue on your fingers when dry

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Small to medium sized, usually fitting comfortably in your palm at 1-2 inches across - smaller than a typical quahog

habitat: Cross-hatched Lucines live in sandy and muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to moderate depths along New England's coast. Their empty shells most commonly wash ashore on sandy beaches, particularly after storms or high tides that stir up the seafloor. Look for them mixed in with other shell debris along the high tide line on beaches from Cape Cod southward.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms, often appearing bright white and well-preserved among other beach debris.
seasonality.summer: Peak beachcombing season when calm weather allows for easier shell hunting, though finding specimens depends on recent wave action.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms frequently bring new shells to shore, making this an excellent time to search for fresh specimens.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms can deposit shells, but harsh conditions make beach searching challenging - look during calm periods after storms pass.

funFact: Cross-hatched Lucines have a special relationship with sulfur bacteria living in their gills - these tiny bacterial partners help the clam process sulfur compounds from decaying organic matter in the sediment, essentially allowing the clam to "eat" what would be toxic to most other animals!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, round clam shells, but the distinctive cross-hatched surface pattern is usually diagnostic - run your finger across the shell surface and you should feel the grid-like ridges that other smooth clam shells lack.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim warning**: With only 13 observations recorded in New England, this species may be at the northern edge of its range or quite rare in our region - don't expect to find these shells on every beach trip, as they're much less common than typical clams like quahogs or steamers.
compareHints: Since this is the only Divalinga species recorded in New England, compare it with other lucine clams in the region, which generally lack the distinctive cross-hatched surface sculpture. Other lucine family members tend to have smoother shells with different ridge patterns - concentric circles rather than intersecting grids. The cross-hatched pattern is really the key distinguishing feature that sets this species apart from its relatives.
